---
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
The \textit{majority digraph} is the directed graph on $[n]$ with an arc from $i$ to $k$ if and only if a majority of voters prefer alternative $i$ over alternative $k$.
A nonempty set \(D\subseteq[n]\) is said to be \textit{dominating} if, for every \(i\in D\) and \(k\in[n]\setminus D\), the majority digraph contains the arc \(i\to k\).
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
The \textit{Smith set} $S$ is the smallest dominating set of alternatives.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:upper bound s=o(n)}
For all integers $1\le s\le n/2$,
\[
\max\bigl\{\mathbb{P}(|S_{m,n}|=s),\,\mathbb{P}(|S_{m,n}|=n-s)\bigr\}
\le \lambda_\ell^s
     \left(\frac{s}{n}\right)^{s(\ell-1)/\ell}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:constant s}
    For any fixed cardinality $s \ge 3$,
\[
\mathbb{P}(|S_{m, n}|=s)=\Theta_{\ell,s} \left(n^{-\frac{s(\ell-1)}{\ell}}\right).
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:upper bound s=theta(n)}
There are constants $C_\ell,N_\ell>0$ such that, for every $n\ge N_\ell$ and integer $3\le s\le n-1$,
\[
\mathbb{P}(|S_{m, n}|=s) \le \binom{n}{s} \left(\zeta_{\ell} \left( \frac sn \right)+C_\ell n^{-1/(m+1)}\right)^n.
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:hamiltonian cycle}
 The probability that the majority digraph has a Hamiltonian cycle is
\[
1-\Theta_{\ell} \left( n^{-(\ell-1)/\ell} \right).
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:lower bound s=theta(n)}
As $n\to\infty$, uniformly over integers $n/\sqrt{\ln n}\le s\le n-1$,
\[
\left(\frac{\mathbb{P}(|S_{m,n}|=s)}{\binom ns}\right)^{1/n}=\zeta_\ell\left(\frac sn\right)+O_\ell\left(n^{-1/(m+1)}\right).
\]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lemma:5}
Let
\begin{equation}
P_s(\mathbf x)
  = \sum_{i=1}^s\sum_{\substack{M\subseteq[m]\\|M|=\ell}}
    \prod_{j\in M}x_{ij}.
\label{eq:analytic-polynomial}
\end{equation}
Then, for all $\mathbf x\in[0,1]^{ms}$,
\[
P_s(\mathbf x)\ge g_s(\mathbf x)
  \ge \frac{P_s(\mathbf x)}{s\binom m\ell}. 
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Alternative $n$ defeats some $i\in[s]$ if and only if there is a set $M\subseteq[m]$ with $|M|=\ell$ such that all voters $j\in M$ prefer $n$ to $i$. For each such pair $(i,M)$, let $\mathcal E_{i,M}$ be this event; equivalently, $X_{nj}<X_{ij}$ for every $j\in M$. Then,
\[
g_s(\mathbf x)
  = \mathbb{P}\Bigg(
    \bigcup_{i\in[s]}\bigcup_{\substack{M\subseteq[m]\\|M|=\ell}}\mathcal E_{i,M}
    \,\Bigg|\,\mathbf x\Bigg).
\]
For any fixed $i$ and $M$, we have
\[
\mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_{i,M}\mid\mathbf x)
  = \mathbb{P}\Bigg(\bigcap_{j\in M}\{x_{ij}>X_{nj}\}\,\Bigg|\,\mathbf x\Bigg).
\]
Given $\mathbf X_{[s]}=\mathbf x$, each $X_{ij}$ with $i\in[s]$ equals $x_{ij}$, while the scores $X_{nj}$ remain independent across voters. Hence the events $\{X_{nj}<x_{ij}\}$ are conditionally independent, and
\[
\mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_{i,M}\mid\mathbf x)
  = \prod_{j\in M}\mathbb{P}(x_{ij}>X_{nj}\mid\mathbf x)
  = \prod_{j\in M}x_{ij}.
\]
Therefore, for all sets $M\subseteq[m]$ with $|M|=\ell$ and $i\in[s]$,
\begin{equation*}
g_s(\mathbf x)\ge \mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_{i,M}\mid\mathbf x)=\prod_{j\in M}x_{ij}.
\end{equation*}
Summing these inequalities over all $s\binom m\ell$ pairs $(M,i)$ gives us
\[
s\binom m\ell g_s(\mathbf x)\ge P_s(\mathbf x),
\qquad
g_s(\mathbf x)\ge\frac{P_s(\mathbf x)}{s\binom m\ell}.
\]
Similarly,
\[
g_s(\mathbf x)
  \le \sum_{i=1}^s\sum_{\substack{M\subseteq[m]\\|M|=\ell}}
      \mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_{i,M}\mid\mathbf x)
  = P_s(\mathbf x).
\]
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lemma:6}
We have
\[
\int_{[0,\infty)^{ms}}e^{-P_s(\mathbf z)}\mathrm{d}\mathbf z=c_\ell^s,
\]
where $c_\ell$ is the finite constant defined in \eqref{eq:constants} and depends only on $\ell$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:s to n-s}
For all $n\in\mathbb N$ and all $1\le s\le n-1$,
\[
\mathbb{P}(\mathcal D_s)
  =\mathbb{P}(\mathcal D_{n-s}).
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $\boldsymbol\pi$ be an $m$-tuple of rankings on $[n]$, and let $\boldsymbol\pi^{\mathrm{rev}}$ be obtained by reversing each ranking. These profiles have equal probability under impartial culture. Furthermore, if alternative $i$ defeats $k$ under $\boldsymbol\pi$, then $k$ defeats $i$ under $\boldsymbol\pi^{\mathrm{rev}}$. Thus, $[s]$ dominates its complement under $\boldsymbol\pi$ if and only if $[n]\setminus[s]$ dominates $[s]$ under $\boldsymbol\pi^{\mathrm{rev}}$. Hence, 
\[
\mathbb{P}(\mathcal D_s)
  =\mathbb{P}([n]\setminus[s]\text{ is a dominating set}).
\]
Furthermore, $[n]\setminus[s]$ and $[n-s]$ have the same cardinality, so they have the same probability of being a dominating set by symmetry, and the conclusion follows.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:Bounding n-s}
For all $1\le s\le n/2$,
\[
\mathbb{P}(|S_{m,n}|=n-s)
  \le\lambda_\ell^s\left(\frac sn\right)^{s(\ell-1)/\ell}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:upperbound_set_size}
Let $L\ge1$ be an integer and $0<\alpha<1$. Suppose $U,V\subseteq[L-1]_0^m$ are sets such that, for every $\mathbf u\in U$ and $\mathbf v\in V$, at least $\ell$ coordinates $j\in[m]$ satisfy $u_j\le v_j$. Then
\[
    |U|^\alpha|V|^{1-\alpha}
    \le (L+1)^m\zeta_\ell(\alpha).
\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:bounding zeta}
For all $\alpha\in[0,1]$,
\[
4^{-m}\le\zeta_\ell(\alpha)\le1.
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:smallConstant}
\[
0<\delta=(2\lambda_\ell)^{-\ell/(\ell-1)}<\frac12.
\]
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:simplified upper bound s=o(n)}
There are constants $K_\ell,N_\ell>0$ such that, for every integer $n\ge N_\ell$ and every integer $3\le s\le\delta n$,
\[
\max\bigl\{\mathbb{P}(|S_{m,n}|=s),\mathbb{P}(|S_{m,n}|=n-s)\bigr\}
\le K_\ell n^{-m/\ell}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:exponential_bound}
For every $\alpha\in[\delta,1-\delta]$,
\[
\zeta_\ell(\alpha)
\le\rho_\ell\alpha^\alpha(1-\alpha)^{1-\alpha}.
\]
Consequently, for every integer $n\ge1$, every integer $s$ with $\delta n\le s\le(1-\delta)n$, and every real $t\ge0$,
\[
\binom ns\bigl(\zeta_\ell(s/n)+t\bigr)^n
\le(\rho_\ell+2t)^n.
\]
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Write $\mathbf z_i=(z_{i1},\ldots,z_{im})$. Using the definitions of $P_s$ in \eqref{eq:analytic-polynomial} and $\sigma_\ell$ in \eqref{eq:sigma} gives
\[
    P_s(\mathbf z)
    =\sum_{i=1}^s\sum_{\substack{M\subseteq[m]\\|M|=\ell}}
        \prod_{j\in M}z_{ij}
    =\sum_{i=1}^s\sigma_\ell(\mathbf z_i).
\]
Hence,
\begin{equation*}
\int_{[0,\infty)^{ms}} e^{-P_s(\mathbf z)}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf z{}=\prod_{i=1}^s
        \int_{[0,\infty)^m}e^{-\sigma_\ell(\mathbf z_i)}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf z_i{}=c_\ell^s.
\end{equation*}
The first equality follows from Tonelli's theorem and the second equality uses the definition of $c_\ell$ in \eqref{eq:constants}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For $1\le s\le n/2$, \eqref{eq:analytic-domination-bound} bounds:
\[
    \binom ns\mathbb{P}(\mathcal D_s)
    \le\lambda_\ell^s\left(\frac{s}{n}\right)^{s(\ell-1)/\ell}.
\]
Thus, by Lemma~\ref{lem:s to n-s},
\[
    \lambda_\ell^s\left(\frac{s}{n}\right)^{s(\ell-1)/\ell}
    \ge\binom ns\mathbb{P}(\mathcal D_s)
    =\binom ns\mathbb{P}(\mathcal D_{n-s})
    =\binom n{n-s}\mathbb{P}(\mathcal D_{n-s})
    \ge\mathbb{P}(|S_{m,n}|=n-s).
\]
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
If either set is empty, the claim is immediate. 
Assume both are nonempty.
Set $\widetilde V=V+(1,\ldots,1)$.
Both $U$ and $\widetilde V$ lie in $[L]_0^m$, and $|\widetilde V|=|V|$. 
For every $\mathbf u\in U$ and $\mathbf v\in V$, the hypothesis gives $u_j<v_j+1$ in at least $\ell$ coordinates. 
Thus the Hamming distance, which counts the coordinates in which two vectors differ, is at least $\ell$ between any point of $U$ and any point of $\widetilde V$. 
Let $N_{\ell-1}(U)$ be the set of points in $[L]_0^m$ at Hamming distance at most $\ell-1$ from some point of $U$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:comb-separated-sets}
    \widetilde V\cap N_{\ell-1}(U)=\varnothing,
    \qquad
    |V|\le (L+1)^m-|N_{\ell-1}(U)|.
\end{equation}
To bound this neighborhood, for each integer $r\in[\ell-1]_0$ let $p_r\in(0,1)$ be the unique solution of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:comb-matched-tail}
    F_{m,p_r}(r)=\frac{|U|}{(L+1)^m}.
\end{equation}
This solution exists because $0<|U|<(L+1)^m$ and $F_{m,p}(r)$ is continuous and strictly decreasing in $p$, from $1$ to $0$. 
Harper's isoperimetric theorem~(\cite[Theorem~3]{HARPER1999285}; see also \cite[Lemma~3]{dai2023fundamental}) implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:comb-hamming-neighborhood}
    \frac{|N_{\ell-1}(U)|}{(L+1)^m}
    \ge\min_{r\in[\ell-1]_0}F_{m,p_r}(r+\ell-1).
\end{equation}
Choose an $r$ attaining the minimum in~\eqref{eq:comb-hamming-neighborhood}. 
Combining this bound with~\eqref{eq:comb-separated-sets} and complementing the binomial tail yields
\begin{align}
\frac{|V|}{(L+1)^m}
&{}\le 1-F_{m,p_r}(r+\ell-1)\notag\\
&{}=F_{m,1-p_r}(\ell-1-r).
\label{eq:comb-complement-bound}
\end{align}
Finally, \eqref{eq:comb-matched-tail}, \eqref{eq:comb-complement-bound}, and the definition~\eqref{eq:zeta} give
\begin{align*}
\frac{|U|^\alpha|V|^{1-\alpha}}{(L+1)^m}
&{}\le F_{m,p_r}(r)^\alpha
    F_{m,1-p_r}(\ell-1-r)^{1-\alpha}\\
&{}\le\zeta_\ell(\alpha),
\end{align*}
which proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For $p\in(0,1)$ and $r\in[\ell-1]_0$, both binomial tails in~\eqref{eq:zeta} lie in $(0,1)$. Thus, for every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, we have $\zeta_\ell(\alpha)\le1$ and
\[
    \zeta_\ell(\alpha)
    \ge\sup_{\substack{p\in(0,1)\\r\in[\ell-1]_0}}
        F_{m,p}(r)\,F_{m,1-p}(\ell-1-r).
\]
Taking $p=\tfrac12$ in~\eqref{eq:binomial-tail}, we have, for every integer $t\in[\ell-1]_0$,
\[
    F_{m,1/2}(t)=2^{-m}\sum_{i=0}^t\binom mi\ge2^{-m}.
\]
Hence
\[
    \zeta_\ell(\alpha)\ge2^{-m}\cdot2^{-m}=4^{-m}.
\]
At the endpoints, taking $r=0$ and letting $p\to1$ or $p\to0$, respectively, also gives $\zeta_\ell(0)=\zeta_\ell(1)=1$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Recall the formula for $\lambda_\ell$ in~\eqref{eq:constants}. 
Let $t=\binom m\ell^{-1/\ell}$. The definition~\eqref{eq:sigma} gives, on $[0,t]^m$,
\[
    \sigma_\ell(\mathbf w)\le\binom m\ell t^\ell=1.
\]
Since $e^{-\sigma_\ell(\mathbf w)}$ is strictly positive,
\[
    c_\ell
    >\int_{[0,t]^m}e^{-\sigma_\ell(\mathbf w)}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf w
    \ge t^m e^{-1}.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
\lambda_\ell&{}>e^{(3\ell-1)/\ell}\binom m\ell^{m/\ell}t^m e^{-1}\\
&{}=e^{(2\ell-1)/\ell}>1.
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\[
    (2\lambda_\ell)^{-\ell/(\ell-1)}
    <2^{-\ell/(\ell-1)}<2^{-1}=\frac12.
\]
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
\label{sec:lemmas-3}
Recall the definitions of $\beta$ and $\delta$ in~\eqref{eq:hamiltonian-cutoffs}. 
Lemma~\ref{lem:smallConstant}, proved below directly from the defining integral in~\eqref{eq:constants}, gives $\delta<1/2$. 
Thus Theorem~\ref{thm:upper bound s=o(n)} applies to every integer $3\le s\le\delta n$, and bounds both probabilities by
\[
B_s=\lambda_\ell^s\left(\frac sn\right)^{\beta s}.
\]
Since $\ell\ge2$, we have $3\beta\ge m/\ell$. Choose $N_\ell\ge256$ so that, for every $n\ge N_\ell$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hamiltonian-large-n-conditions}
\lambda_\ell n^{-3\beta/4}\le1,
\qquad
2^{-n^{1/4}}\le n^{-m/\ell}.
\end{equation}
Such a threshold depends only on $\ell$: the first left-hand side in~\eqref{eq:hamiltonian-large-n-conditions} tends to zero, and $n^{1/4}/\ln n\to\infty$ gives its second inequality. We now consider three exhaustive ranges of integer $s$. If $s=3$, then
\begin{align*}
B_3&{}=\lambda_\ell^3 3^{3\beta}n^{-3\beta}\\
&{}\le(3\lambda_\ell)^3n^{-m/\ell}.
\end{align*}
If $4\le s\le n^{1/4}$, then $s/n\le n^{-3/4}$ and~\eqref{eq:hamiltonian-large-n-conditions} makes the base in the following power at most one. Hence,
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_s
&\le\bigl(\lambda_\ell n^{-3\beta/4}\bigr)^s
 \le\bigl(\lambda_\ell n^{-3\beta/4}\bigr)^4\\
&=\lambda_\ell^4n^{-3\beta}
 \le\lambda_\ell^4n^{-m/\ell}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally, if $n^{1/4}<s\le\delta n$, then $\lambda_\ell(s/n)^\beta\le\lambda_\ell\delta^\beta=1/2$ by~\eqref{eq:hamiltonian-cutoffs}. 
Together with~\eqref{eq:hamiltonian-large-n-conditions}, this gives
\[
B_s\le2^{-s}\le2^{-n^{1/4}}\le n^{-m/\ell}.
\]
Thus $K_\ell=\max\{(3\lambda_\ell)^3,\lambda_\ell^4,1\}$ works simultaneously for every integer in the stated range.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:method of types}
For integers $n\ge1$ and $0\le s\le n$, with $\alpha=s/n$,
\[
    \binom ns\le e^{nh(\alpha)}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Fix $\alpha\in[\delta,1-\delta]$. 
Abbreviate the two binomial tails involved in \eqref{eq:zeta} by
\[
    a_r(p)=F_{m,p}(r),
    \qquad
    b_r(p)=F_{m,1-p}(\ell-1-r).
\]
Recall from~\eqref{eq:central-constants} that
\[
    \epsilon_\ell
    =\min\left\{\frac1{\ell\binom m\ell},
        \frac{\delta(1-\delta)^{(1-\delta)/\delta}}2\right\},
\]
which satisfies $0<\epsilon_\ell<\delta/2<1/4$. 
For every integer $r\in[\ell-1]_0$, we divide into three cases according to whether $p$ lies in $(0,\epsilon_\ell)$, $[\epsilon_\ell,1-\epsilon_\ell]$, or $(1-\epsilon_\ell,1)$.

We begin with $p\in[\epsilon_\ell,1-\epsilon_\ell]$. Consider
\[
    a_r(p)+b_r(p)
    =1-\sum_{i=r+1}^{r+\ell-1}\binom mi p^i(1-p)^{m-i}.
\]
Because $\ell-1\ge1$, the sum contains its $i=r+1$ term. For $r\in[\ell-1]_0$ and $p\in[\epsilon_\ell,1-\epsilon_\ell]$,
\begin{align}
a_r(p)+b_r(p)&{}\le1-\binom m{r+1}p^{r+1}(1-p)^{m-r-1}\notag\\
&{}\le1-p^{r+1}(1-p)^{m-r-1}{}\le1-\epsilon_\ell^m.
\label{eq:central-middle-gap}
\end{align}
For $x,y\ge0$, weighted AM--GM gives $(x/\alpha)^\alpha(y/(1-\alpha))^{1-\alpha}\le x+y$, or $x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\le(x+y)e^{-h(\alpha)}$. 
Applying this to~\eqref{eq:central-middle-gap} yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:central-middle-product}
    a_r(p)^\alpha b_r(p)^{1-\alpha}
    \le(1-\epsilon_\ell^m)e^{-h(\alpha)}
    \qquad\text{for }p\in[\epsilon_\ell,1-\epsilon_\ell].
\end{equation}

If $p<\epsilon_\ell$, then
\begin{align*}
b_r(p)&{}=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1-r}\binom mi(1-p)^i p^{m-i}\\
&{}\le\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1-r}\binom m\ell p^{m-i}{}\le\ell\binom m\ell p^\ell
    <\epsilon_\ell^\ell\ell\binom m\ell.
\end{align*}
Since $\ell\ge2$ and $0<\epsilon_\ell<1$, we have $\epsilon_\ell^{\ell-1}\le\epsilon_\ell\le1/(\ell\binom m\ell)$. 
Consequently $b_r(p)<\epsilon_\ell$. As $a_r(p)\le1$,
\begin{align}
a_r(p)^\alpha b_r(p)^{1-\alpha}&{}\le\epsilon_\ell^{1-\alpha}{}\le\left(\frac{\delta(1-\delta)^{(1-\delta)/\delta}}2\right)^{1-\alpha}.
\label{eq:central-small-p-product}
\end{align}
To bound the right-hand side of~\eqref{eq:central-small-p-product}, note that $f(\alpha)=(1-\alpha)\alpha^{\alpha/(1-\alpha)}$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,1)$, since $(\ln f)'(\alpha)=\ln\alpha/(1-\alpha)^2<0$. Since $\alpha\le1-\delta$,
\begin{align}
\left(\frac{\delta(1-\delta)^{(1-\delta)/\delta}}2\right)^{1-\alpha}&{}\le\left(\frac{(1-\alpha)\alpha^{\alpha/(1-\alpha)}}2\right)^{1-\alpha}\notag\\
&{}=2^{-(1-\alpha)}e^{-h(\alpha)}{}\le2^{-\delta}e^{-h(\alpha)}.
\label{eq:central-small-p-entropy}
\end{align}

Finally, if $p>1-\epsilon_\ell$, replacing $(p,r,\alpha)$ by $(1-p,\ell-1-r,1-\alpha)$ interchanges $a_r(p)$ and $b_r(p)$, so the preceding argument applies unchanged and gives $a_r(p)^\alpha b_r(p)^{1-\alpha}\le2^{-\delta}e^{-h(\alpha)}$.
Recall $\rho_\ell$ from~\eqref{eq:central-constants}. The bounds~\eqref{eq:central-middle-product} and~\eqref{eq:central-small-p-product}--\eqref{eq:central-small-p-entropy}, together with this symmetry argument, are uniform in $p$, the integer $r$, and $\alpha\in[\delta,1-\delta]$. 
Taking the supremum in~\eqref{eq:zeta} therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:central-zeta-gap}
    \zeta_\ell(\alpha)
    =\sup_{\substack{p\in(0,1)\\r\in[\ell-1]_0}}
        a_r(p)^\alpha b_r(p)^{1-\alpha}
    \le\rho_\ell e^{-h(\alpha)}.
\end{equation}
For the second assertion, let $n,s$ satisfy the stated integer restrictions, set $\alpha=s/n$, and fix any $t\ge0$. Lemma~\ref{lem:method of types} and~\eqref{eq:central-zeta-gap} imply
\begin{align*}
\binom ns\bigl(\zeta_\ell(\alpha)+t\bigr)^n
&{}\le e^{nh(\alpha)}
    \bigl(\rho_\ell e^{-h(\alpha)}+t\bigr)^n\\
&{}=\bigl(\rho_\ell+t e^{h(\alpha)}\bigr)^n\\
&{}\le(\rho_\ell+2t)^n.
\end{align*}
The final inequality follows from $h(\alpha)\le\ln2$, the maximum attained at $\alpha=1/2$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
